bib.title: Agent-as-a-Router: Agentic Model Routing for Coding Tasks

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Agent-as-a-Router: Agentic Model Routing for Coding Tasks", Pengfei Zhou et al. (NUS, DAMO/Alibaba, others). Preprint, arXiv 2606.22902v3, header dated 2026-06-22 (v3 26 Jun 2026). First author Zhou, June 2026. No venue. Code and benchmark: github.com/LanceZPF/agent-as-a-router.
COVERAGE: 39 of 39 pages read (113,708 chars). Pages 30-39 are task-example dumps (Figs 12-21), skimmed only. The references were skimmed.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Routing is framed as a Context-Action-Feedback loop. The router sees context (prompt, metadata, memory), picks a model, gets verified score and cost, and writes that back into memory. The authors call it a contextual bandit and use cumulative regret as the streaming metric.
  number: none (formal)
  setup: Eq. 1, 7; model pool of 8; stream of N tasks
  quote: "formalizing routing as a Context-Action-Feedback (C-A-F) loop, in which each loop's verified outcome enters the next loop's context"
  where: p2 (Sec 1), p4 (Sec 3.2)
- Information deficit, not reasoning, limits an LLM router. Adding per-dimension performance statistics to a zero-shot Claude Sonnet 4.6 router raises AvgPerf from 41.41 to 47.74, a 15.3% relative gain. This beats DimensionBest (47.50).
  number: 41.41 -> 47.74 (+15.3%); oracle 57.00
  setup: Claude Sonnet 4.6 as router, 2,919 ID test tasks; stats from a 7,080-task probing set; 8 candidate models
  quote: "With only the zero-shot prompt Vanilla router scores 41.41, and adding per-dimension performance statistics from a held-out probing set (+Perf stats) improves the score to 47.74, a +15.3% relative gain over Vanilla."
  where: p2; Table 1 p3
  Caveat: +Perf stats had worse Perf/$ (1.71 vs 1.97 Vanilla).
- ACRouter has the lowest cumulative regret in distribution and on the OOD agentic set.
  number: ID AvgPerf 49.98 (DimensionBest 47.50), CumReg 205.5 (next best 277.4). OOD AvgPerf 62.50, CumReg 17.0 (Always-Opus 57.14 / 26.7).
  setup: ID n=2,919 single-turn tasks; OOD n=176 agentic tasks (SWE-bench Verified, LongCLI-Bench, FeatureBench, SWE-CI); mini-swe-agent capped at 40 steps. CumReg uses reward = score - 0.1*cost.
  quote: "On the ID test, ACRouter reaches the highest AvgPerf (49.98%) and the lowest cumulative regret (205.5), beating DimensionBest with a full dimension-level prior by 2.48% AvgPerf."
  where: p9, Table 3
- Static trained routers fail out of distribution. They are near DimensionBest in distribution but score below Random on OOD.
  number: OOD AvgPerf 8.93-21.43% vs Random 31.25%
  setup: LogReg, TF-IDF+MLP, RouteLLM-MF/BERT trained on the probing set. The fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B is the exception at 55.36%.
  quote: "their OOD AvgPerf drops sharply to 8.93%–21.43%, even lower than Random (31.25%)."
  where: p10
- Online bandits adapt but lag ACRouter.
  number: LinUCB 49.82 / LinTS 46.43 OOD; CumReg 31.1 / 35.9
  quote: "contextual bandits (LinUCB, LinTS) keep updating online and also survive better, reaching 49.82% / 46.43% OOD"
  where: p10, Table 3
- Cost: ACRouter is cheaper than always using the strongest model.
  number: ID $13.21 vs Always-Opus $34.02; Perf/$ 3.79 vs 1.29. OOD $52.97 vs $89.28; Perf/$ 1.18 vs 0.64.
  setup: API prices (Table 6); router tokens self-hosted at $0.054/M, derived from H100 at $6.88/hr and ~35,094 tok/s
  quote: "Always-Opus pays the most ($34.02) yet trails ACRouter by 6.15 AvgPerf points and accumulates 387.1 regret"
  where: p26-27, Tables 12-13
- No model dominates. Opus 4.6 has the best average (42.9%) but loses on algorithms to GLM-5 (47.2 vs 25.4), on test generation to Qwen3-Max (82.7 vs 39.2) and on data science to Kimi-K2.5 (18.4 vs 14.2). Opus costs about 12x Kimi-K2.5.
  setup: 7,080-task probing set, 9 dimensions
  quote: "Claude Opus 4.6 achieves the highest average (42.9%) but is outperformed on algorithm design by GLM-5 (47.2% vs. 25.4%, an 86% relative improvement)"
  where: p8
- Coding ability does not equal routing ability. As routers, all 8 LLMs stay below DimensionBest. Opus 4.6 ranks last (39.27 zero-shot). Few-shot does not reliably help. Online memory with an LLM router is mixed.
  setup: Table 7, ID test, 0-shot / 3-shot / "agent online" with a 200-task warm-up
  quote: "coding ability≠ routing ability: all 8 LLM routers remain below DimensionBest, and Claude Opus 4.6 ranks last in both 0-shot and 3-shot"
  where: p22
- Fine-tuning gates router quality; size does not. Five Qwen3.5 sizes from 0.8B to 27B land at 46.21-46.74 AvgPerf. Unfine-tuned base models fall back to the always-Sonnet floor (0.4131).
  quote: "Across a ∼ 30× parameter range, AvgPerf moves only ∼ 0.5 points (46.21−46.74)."
  where: p22
- Dimension identity alone captures only about 27% of the entropy of the oracle's choice. The rest is per-task content, which is why embedding-kNN memory helps.
  quote: "dimension identity captures roughly 27% of the entropy of 𝑦𝑡"
  where: p24 (D.3)
- On OOD, a standalone GPT-5.4 backend resolves 75.00% (132/176), above ACRouter's 62.50 and near the oracle's 75.89.
  quote: "the updated GPT-5.4 run resolves 132/176 = 75.00% of tasks"
  where: p28, Table 14. This undercuts the OOD win. ACRouter beats the baselines in its own table, not the best single model that was later added.

ACRouter design (for the note): Orchestrator = fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B + heuristics by weighted vote, with the DimensionBest prior and the top-10 kNN neighbours. Verifier = AST parse, sandbox run, self-consistency, LLM-judge and in-prompt tests, combined by type-specific weights summing to 1. Memory = embedding store (voyage-code-3 / BGE-large), cosine kNN k=10, threshold 0.5, FIFO-bounded at 20K, warm-started on 200 val tasks.

LIMITS
- Authors concede (p11): provider cache hit rates are unobservable, so cost is only a secondary reference. The OOD run uses a 40-step cap instead of 250. Only one instantiation (LLM policy + kNN memory) was tried, and parameter-level memory is untested.
- My reading: the OOD set is 176 tasks, and I saw no seeds or confidence intervals except "5-seed avg" for the bandits. GLM-5 has ~14.5% missing tasks scored as 0, which depresses its numbers. Models were frontier as of early 2026 and have dated. The oracle uses the full outcome matrix, so regret is offline replay, not live deployment. The Verifier is itself a cost, and ACRouter spends more per task than cheap classifiers (ID Perf/$ 3.79 vs about 6).
- The "self-evolving" claim covers a routing policy plus a memory store. Weights are not updated. Only the memory changes.

BUILDS ON: contextual bandits (Li, Chu, Langford, Schapire 2010 LinUCB; Agrawal & Goyal 2013 LinTS; Lattimore & Szepesvari 2020). Routing work: RouteLLM (Ong et al.), FrugalGPT (Chen et al.), AutoMix (Aggarwal et al. 2024), Hybrid LLM (Ding et al. 2024), LLMRouterBench (Li et al. 2026), MasRouter (Yue et al. 2025). Harness: mini-swe-agent, SWE-bench (Jimenez et al.), LoRA, SGLang.

CODE: none. The only snippet is the router prompt (p19): "You are a coding task router. Your objective is to maximize the performance-cost trade-off... Respond with JSON: {"model": "...", "reasoning": "..."}". Eq. 2: r = e1*s + e2*kappa with (e1, e2) = (1, -0.1). Eq. 7: CumReg = sum over tasks of (r* - r).

FIGURES (page)
- Fig 1 (p3): static heuristic vs trained policy vs agent-as-router. Shows the loop idea quickly.
- Fig 2 (p6): ACRouter architecture with a worked weighted-vote example (Kimi-K2.5 wins with 1.47). Best slide candidate.
- Fig 5 (p10): cumulative regret curves, ID and OOD. Static routers diverge, ACRouter flattens.
- Fig 6 (p10): cost-performance Pareto frontier.
- Fig 4 (p8): model x dimension heatmap and cost. Shows why routing pays off.
- Table 4 (p16): which of Orchestrator, Verifier, Memory each method family has. Useful as an ablation map.

FIT: Weak for 08-self-improving-loops. The loop only learns a model-choice memory, with no code, prompt or skill evolution. A short mention works as an example of "experience memory + verifier feedback beats a frozen prior under distribution shift". It fits better in model routing within a loop, and in budgets and cost. The evidence there is that Always-Opus costs 2.6x more than ACRouter ID, and that routers cost far less than the strongest model. Sec E.3 itself lists effort, tool and sub-agent routing as the same loop.

PROBLEMS: none significant. No embedded instructions. Extraction of the tables and figure text was clean. The heatmap numbers in Fig 4 are scrambled but unused. The abstract has no month and the header gives only "2026-06-22".
